The frog makes a round trip: it starts at the first stone, reaches the last stone, and returns to the first stone. Each stone may be used **at most once** across both directions (the first and last stones are shared by both legs). The cost is the longest single jump in the whole trip, and we minimize that cost.

**Example 1:** `stones = [0,2,5,6,7]`. Going out via `0 → 5 → 7` (jumps 5, 2) and returning via `7 → 6 → 2 → 0` (jumps 1, 4, 2) gives cost 5. Any plan needs some jump covering a span of 5 because with smaller jumps you cannot cover all stones within budget — so the answer is 5.

**Example 2:** `stones = [0,3,9]`. The only sensible trip is `0 → 9` and back, costing 9 twice; splitting differently still forces a jump of 9 somewhere.

Constraints ($n \le 10^5$, positions up to $10^9$) rule out exponential enumeration of assignments but allow an $O(n)$ or $O(n \log n)$ pass, hinting at a greedy/binary-search structure.
k: The round trip splits stones into two increasing sequences (outbound and return), each starting at stones[0] and ending at stones[n-1]; the cost is the largest adjacent gap inside either sequence.
In an optimal split, consecutive stones on the same path are 2 apart in index: if one path skips only one stone, that stone goes to the other path, so no gap of width > 2 in index is ever needed.
Therefore the answer is simply the maximum of stones[i+2] - stones[i] over all i (or stones[1]-stones[0] when n == 2).

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search on the Answer + Greedy Feasibility Check
a.i: The cost is monotone: if cost $k$ is achievable, any $k' > k$ is too. So binary search on $k$. To test $k$, sweep stones left to right keeping the last stone used by each of the two paths; assign each new stone to whichever path's last stone is farther back (so its jump fits), preferring the path with the larger last position when both fit. This greedy assignment is safe because giving the stone to the more constrained path never helps.
s: Set search range lo = 0, hi = stones[n-1] - stones[0] (direct jump there and back).
For a candidate k, run the greedy check: maintain last positions a and b of the two paths.
For each next stone s: if it fits after neither a nor b, fail; if it fits after both, move the path with the larger last position to s; otherwise move the fitting path.
If the check passes, try smaller k; otherwise increase k.
a.t: O(n log M) where M = stones[n-1] - stones[0] — each feasibility check is O(n), done O(log M) times.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.i: Think of the trip as two increasing chains over the sorted stones. If a chain jumps over two or more intermediate stones, one of those skipped stones could be inserted into the other chain without increasing any jump length beyond the current maximum — so an optimal solution exists where each chain advances by index steps of at most 2. Hence every jump has length at most max(stones[i+2]-stones[i]), and this bound is achievable by alternating stones between the outbound and return paths (e.g., even indices one way, odd indices the other). The answer is therefore just the maximum of stones[i+2]-stones[i], or stones[1]-stones[0] for n == 2.
s: For each i from 0 to n-3, update ans = max(ans, stones[i+2] - stones[i]).
a.t: O(n) — single linear scan computing stones[i+2] - stones[i].

w: In an interview, mention the binary-search-on-answer idea to show structured thinking, then derive the O(n) formula — interviewers love the exchange argument showing index gaps of 2 suffice. Pitfalls: forgetting the n == 2 case (loop range would be empty); assuming each direction must visit contiguous stones (it need not); misreading 'at most once' as 'exactly once per direction'. Edge cases: two stones, three stones, tightly packed stones (answer may be small like 1–2). Follow-ups: what if stones were unsorted (sort first, same complexity plus O(n log n)); what if the frog could revisit stones (answer becomes stones[last]-stones[first]); prove optimality formally via the exchange argument.
